Fact: Volkswagen was founded on May 28, 1937, by the German Labour Front, known as the Deutsche Arbeitsfront.
The original purpose of the company was to mass-produce an affordable, fuel-efficient car for the German working class.
The official original name of the company in Nazi Germany was Gesellschaft zur Vorbereitung des Deutschen Volkswagen mbH.
The company was shortened to Volkswagenwerk GmbH in July 1938.
The iconic design of the Volkswagen Beetle was created by Austro-Hungarian automotive engineer Ferdinand Porsche.
Adolf Hitler heavily promoted the "People's Car" project, demanding it carry two adults and three children at speeds up to 100 km/h while costing no more than 990 Reichsmarks.
Ferdinand Porsche built the initial prototypes, known as the "KdF-Wagen" (Kraft durch Freude, or Strength Through Joy).
The first factory for the company was established in a brand-new planned town initially called Stadt des KdF-Wagens, which was later renamed Wolfsburg.
Construction of the massive Wolfsburg factory began in 1938, but very few KdF-Wagens were built for civilians before World War II intervened.
With the outbreak of World War II in 1939, production at the Wolfsburg plant was forcefully shifted away from consumer cars to military vehicles.
The primary military vehicle produced at the plant was the Type 82 Kübelwagen, a light military utility vehicle based on the Beetle's mechanical platform.
Volkswagen also produced the Schwimmwagen, an amphibious four-wheel-drive variant powered by the air-cooled flat-four engine.
During the war, the factory also manufactured the V-1 flying bomb, utilizing thousands of forced laborers, concentration camp prisoners, and foreign workers under brutal conditions.
By the end of World War II in 1945, the Wolfsburg factory was heavily damaged by Allied bombing raids.
Following Germany's surrender, the British Army took control of the ruined Wolfsburg plant under the command of Major Ivan Hirst.
Major Hirst recognized the potential of the remaining factory equipment and ordered the factory to begin rebuilding civilian Beetles for British military transport.
The British military administration officially renamed the town Wolfsburg in May 1945.
In 1946, the plant achieved a milestone of producing 1,000 cars a month, an astonishing feat given the rubble and material shortages.
Volkswagen manufactured its 10,000th car in March 1946, less than a year after the British takeover.
In 1948, Heinz Nordhoff was appointed general director of Volkswagen, bringing vital leadership that would steer the company's global expansion.
In October 1949, the British handed full control of Volkswagen back to the German government and the state of Lower Saxony.
The Volkswagen logo, featuring a stacked V and W inside a circle, evolved from initial gear-like motifs into a clean, modern corporate badge.
The Volkswagen Beetle was officially designated internally as the Type 1.
In 1950, Volkswagen expanded its lineup beyond the Beetle by introducing the Type 2, better known as the Transporter, Microbus, or Kombi.
The Type 2 Transporter was conceptualized by Dutch Volkswagen importer Ben Pon, who sketched a delivery van based on the Beetle chassis.
The Volkswagen Beetle surpassed 100,000 total units produced in 1950.
In 1951, Volkswagen began exporting the Beetle to international markets, beginning a massive global export wave.
Volkswagen of America was established in 1955 to handle the surging popularity of the Beetle and Microbus in the United States.
By August 1955, the one-millionth Volkswagen Beetle rolled off the assembly line in Wolfsburg.
In 1955, industrial designer Wilhelm Karmann began producing the Karmann Ghia, a stylish sports coupe blending Italian styling by Carrozzeria Ghia with Beetle mechanicals.
The Karmann Ghia convertible variant was introduced in 1957, expanding the sporty appeal of the brand.
In 1961, Volkswagen introduced the Type 3, known as the Karmann Ghia successor line, featuring notchback, fastback, and squareback body styles.
The Type 3 introduced a "flat" version of the air-cooled boxer engine to maximize cargo space under the rear floorboards.
Volkswagen purchased Auto Union from Daimler-Benz in 1964, gaining ownership of the Audi brand and vital water-cooled engine technology.
In 1965, the millionth Volkswagen was sold in the United States alone.
Volkswagen acquired NSU Motorenwerke AG in 1969, merging it with Auto Union to form Audi NSU Auto Union AG.
In 1968, the Type 4 (Volkswagen 411/412) was introduced, featuring a unibody construction and a larger air-cooled engine.
The Volkswagen Beetle finally surpassed the long-standing production record of the Ford Model T on February 17, 1972, with Beetle number 15,007,034 built.
To celebrate the production record, Volkswagen released a special edition model called the "Super Beetle" 1302/1303 series featuring MacPherson strut front suspension.

Recognizing that rear-engine, air-cooled technology was reaching the end of its regulatory and market life, Volkswagen initiated development of front-wheel-drive, water-cooled vehicles in the early 1970s.
The Audi acquisition provided the engineering blueprint for the revolutionary water-cooled front-wheel-drive platforms that would save the company.
In 1973, Volkswagen launched the Passat, a modern front-wheel-drive hatchback and estate developed from Audi's engineering base.
In 1974, Volkswagen introduced the Scirocco, a sporty compact coupe styled by Giorgetto Giugiaro.
On March 29, 1974, the very last German-built Beetle rolled off the Wolfsburg production line, though production continued elsewhere.
In May 1974, Volkswagen introduced the Golf (marketed as the Rabbit in North America), replacing the Beetle as the brand's volume hatchback.
The Golf was designed by legendary Italian automotive designer Giorgetto Giugiaro.
The Golf quickly became a massive global success, establishing the standard for the modern hot hatchback category.
In 1976, Volkswagen launched the high-performance Golf GTI, revolutionizing affordable sports cars.
In 1975, Volkswagen introduced the Polo, a smaller, highly economical supermini based on the Audi 50.
Despite the shift to water-cooled models, Volkswagen continued to manufacture air-cooled Beetles, buses, and specialized vehicles in international plants.
Volkswagen established production facilities outside Germany early on, including Volkswagen do Brasil, founded in 1953.
Volkswagen de México began operations in Puebla, Mexico, in the 1960s, eventually becoming the ultimate global stronghold for air-cooled Beetle production.
The Volkswagen Beetle was affectionately given numerous nicknames worldwide, including "Bug," "Vocho," "Fusca," "Coccinelle," and "Käfer."
The air-cooled flat-four engine powering the classic Volkswagen lineup utilized horizontally opposed cylinders, making it compact and balanced.
Classic air-cooled Volkswagen engines relied on cooling fins on the cylinder heads and a specialized engine cooling fan shroud driven by the generator/alternator belt.
The early air-cooled engines featured a displacement of 1,100cc and produced a modest 25 horsepower.
Engine displacement gradually increased over the decades to 1,200cc, 1,300cc, 1,500cc, and eventually 1,600cc in standard late-model configurations.
The electrical system on early air-cooled Volkswagens operated on 6 volts until switching to 12 volts in the late 1960s.
The classic Volkswagen transmission used a transaxle layout combining the manual gearbox and differential into a single housing.
Early Beetles used split-rear windows until 1953, when a larger oval window was introduced.
In 1958, the Beetle rear window was enlarged again into a square panoramic shape that persisted through the end of standard production.
The Type 2 Microbus evolved significantly, moving from the iconic "Split-Screen" (Splittie) design produced until 1967 to the "Bay-Window" model introduced for the 1968 model year.
The Bay-Window Transporter featured a wraparound single-piece windshield and updated suspension for improved highway stability.
In 1979, Volkswagen introduced the third-generation Transporter, known as the T3 or Vanagon in North America.
The T3 Vanagon initially utilized air-cooled flat-four engines before transitioning to water-cooled boxer engines in the 1980s, marking the end of air-cooled utility vehicles in Europe.
The Volkswagen Karmann Ghia continued production through 1974, with over 445,000 units built across coupe and convertible versions.
The Beetle convertible, also built by Karmann, remained in production in Germany long after the sedan left Wolfsburg, ending in January 1980.
As production in Germany wound down, Beetle manufacturing shifted heavily to plants in Mexico and Brazil.
In Brazil, Volkswagen produced air-cooled models tailored to local markets, including the Brasília, Variant, and SP2 sports car.
The Volkswagen SP2, built in Brazil during the early 1970s, is widely regarded as one of the most stylish air-cooled cars ever built, though it was famously underpowered.
The Brazilian air-cooled engine lineup also included the rugged Volkswagen Thing (sold as the Pescador or Type 181 in Europe and Safari in Mexico).
The Type 181 was a civilian derivative of military vehicles, featuring four doors, a folding top, and removable side windows on a modified Beetle floorpan.
Volkswagen of America imported the Type 181 as the "Thing" for the 1973 and 1974 model years before safety regulations halted sales.
The classic air-cooled Beetle reached its 20-millionth production milestone in May 1981 at the Puebla plant in Mexico.
In Brazil, air-cooled Beetle production was temporarily halted in 1986, only to be famously restarted in 1993 at the request of Brazilian President Itamar Franco.
These revived Brazilian Beetles, known as "Fusca Itamar," were produced until 1996.
In Mexico, the Beetle (locally called the "Vocho") became an indispensable part of Mexican culture, serving as the ubiquitous green-and-white Mexico City taxi for decades.
Mexican-built air-cooled Beetles incorporated various modern upgrades over the years, including electronic fuel injection starting in the 1993 model year.
The fuel-injected Mexican air-cooled engine utilized a sophisticated Digifant ECU system, catalytic converters, and hydraulic valve lifters to meet stringent emissions standards.
Despite fuel injection, the fundamental architecture of the air-cooled flat-four boxer engine remained completely intact from its 1930s origins.
The very last air-cooled Volkswagen Beetle ever built rolled off the assembly line at the Puebla, Mexico factory on July 30, 2003.
This final car, painted in a special "Harvest Moon Beige" color, was driven straight off the line and loaded onto a transport truck bound for the Volkswagen museum in Wolfsburg.

To commemorate the end of an era, Volkswagen produced a limited run of 3,000 "Ultima Edición" (Last Edition) Beetles in Mexico for the 2004 model year, featuring whitewall tires, chrome trim, and special paint.
Over the entire 65-year production run from 1938 to 2003, a staggering total of 21,529,464 classic air-cooled Beetles were manufactured worldwide.
The air-cooled Volkswagen engine platform spawned an entire aftermarket industry dedicated to performance tuning, dune buggies, and custom hot rods.
Bruce Meyers famously created the Meyers Manx dune buggy in 1964 using a shortened classic Volkswagen Beetle floorpan and chassis.
The simplicity of the air-cooled Volkswagen drivetrain made it a favorite for kit cars, trikes, and ultralight aircraft.
The engine features an aluminum-alloy crankcase holding a forged steel crankshaft running in four main bearings.
The cylinders are cast iron with detachable aluminum cylinder heads housing overhead valves operated by pushrods from a centrally located camshaft.
Lubrication on the air-cooled engine relies on a gear-type oil pump driven directly by the camshaft, utilizing an internal oil cooler mounted inside the fan shroud.
The ignition system on traditional air-cooled Volkswagens relied on a mechanical distributor driven by the camshaft gear.
Fuel delivery on most classic air-cooled models was handled by a single downdraft Solex carburetor mounted atop the intake manifold.
High-performance air-cooled builders frequently upgraded to dual carburetor setups, such as Weber IDFs or Dellorto DRLAs, to increase airflow and power output.
The exhaust system on a stock Beetle featured "j-tubes" or heat exchangers that captured warmth from the exhaust gases to heat the vehicle's interior.
The clutch on air-cooled Volkswagens operated via a steel cable connected to the foot pedal, engaging a single-dry-disc clutch assembly.
The suspension on classic Beetles initially utilized dual torsion bars front and rear, giving the car its characteristic independent suspension setup.
Later models, such as the Super Beetle, transitioned to coil-spring MacPherson struts in the front while retaining trailing arms and torsion bars in the rear.
Steering on classic Volkswagens utilized a worm-and-roller steering box that required periodic mechanical adjustment to eliminate play.
Brakes on early models were four-wheel mechanical drums, which were upgraded to hydraulic drum brakes in the 1950s and optional front disc brakes in later years.
The fuel tank on classic air-cooled Beetles was positioned in the front luggage compartment beneath the hood, directly ahead of the spare tire.
The spare tire on a classic Beetle was mounted flat in the front trunk and dual-purposed as a pressure reservoir for the windshield washer system.
The windshield washer pump on many classic Volkswagens was powered entirely by air pressure bled from the spare tire.
The fuel gauge on early Beetles did not exist; drivers relied on a mechanical reserve valve on the fuel petcock under the dashboard to switch to reserve fuel.
Later classic Beetles incorporated an electric fuel gauge integrated directly into the single central speedometer housing.
The interior of a classic Beetle was famously spartan, featuring painted metal dashboards, rubber floor mats, and simple vinyl seats.
Sound deadening was minimal, resulting in the distinctive, unmistakable hum of the air-cooled boxer engine echoing from the rear.
The heater boxes on air-cooled Volkswagens were notorious for occasionally carrying exhaust odors into the cabin if the internal seals failed.
The lack of a water-cooling system meant classic Volkswagens had no radiator, water pump, or antifreeze, simplifying winter maintenance while requiring vigilant oil changes.
The oil filter on stock air-cooled Volkswagen engines was simply a wire-mesh oil strainer screen located at the bottom of the crankcase, supplemented later by a bypass oil filtration system.
Valve adjustments on air-cooled Volkswagens were a routine maintenance task recommended every 3,000 to 5,000 miles using feeler gauges.
The firing order for all standard air-cooled Volkswagen flat-four engines is 1-4-3-2.

The engine could easily be removed from the car by unbolting four main fasteners, disconnecting the electrical wires, fuel line, and throttle cable, allowing a mechanic to drop the engine out the back in under an hour.
Volkswagen's post-war success became a cornerstone of the German economic miracle, known as the Wirtschaftswunder.
The company's headquarters and primary manufacturing plant in Wolfsburg remains one of the largest automotive manufacturing complexes in the world.
The Wolfsburg plant features massive brick power stations that originally powered both the factory and the surrounding city.
Volkswagen established Autostadt, a massive visitor attraction and delivery center adjacent to the Wolfsburg factory, featuring automotive museums and glass delivery towers.
In the 1950s, Volkswagen advertising agency Doyle Dane Bernbach (DDB) launched the groundbreaking "Think Small" campaign, which revolutionized automotive marketing.
The "Think Small" advertisements embraced the Beetle's small size, quirky looks, and economy, turning perceived weaknesses into badge-of-honor strengths.
Another famous DDB ad for the Beetle used the headline "Lemon," highlighting strict quality control that rejected a car because of a minor blemish.
The cultural footprint of the Beetle expanded dramatically in 1968 when a pearl-white 1963 Sunroof Beetle starred in the Walt Disney film *The Love Bug*, named "Herbie."
Herbie became a global cinematic icon, spawning an entire franchise of films and cementing the Beetle's friendly, personable image in popular culture.
The air-cooled Volkswagen Microbus became the definitive transport vehicle for the 1960s counterculture and hippie movement.
Painted in vibrant psychedelic colors, the Type 2 bus symbolized freedom, road trips, and communal travel.
Music festivals like Woodstock cemented the image of the Volkswagen bus as an enduring symbol of peace and youth culture.
In South Africa, Volkswagen produced a unique variant called the "Jurgens" camper conversion, alongside specialized local utility models.
Australia built its own unique history of air-cooled Volkswagens, including locally assembled Beetles and utility versions known as "Country Buggies."
The Volkswagen Country Buggy, produced in Australia from 1967 to 1969, featured a utilitarian flat-paneled steel body built on a Beetle floorpan.
In Mexico, the air-cooled engine powered the VW Combi (Type 2) well into the 21st century, serving as mass transit across Mexican cities.
Mexican production of the air-cooled Type 2 bus continued until late 2001, outlasting European production by decades.
The final air-cooled Type 2 bus produced in Mexico was celebrated with a special "Last Edition" series featuring two-tone paint and luxury trim.
Volkswagen's transition to water-cooled engines in the 1970s ensured the company's survival as safety and emissions regulations tightened globally.
The water-cooled front-wheel-drive platform debuted by the Passat and Golf set the blueprint for modern automobile layout standards.
The Golf nameplate went on to become one of the best-selling cars in automotive history, spanning eight generations.
Despite the massive shift toward modern water-cooled lineups, the air-cooled community grew increasingly passionate, preserving millions of classic Beetles and buses.
Restoration parts for air-cooled Volkswagens became widely available through dedicated specialty suppliers, ensuring cars built in the 1950s and 60s remain roadworthy today.
The Volkswagen air-cooled engine block is made of magnesium alloy rather than standard aluminum or cast iron, saving precious weight.
The cooling fan mounted atop the generator housing draws air through the engine compartment and forces it down across the cylinder cooling fins via metal tinware.
Proper engine tinware and rubber seals around the perimeter of the engine bay are critical; missing tin causes hot exhaust air to recirculate, leading to rapid overheating.
The classic Volkswagen suspension uses torsion leaf springs housed inside thick steel tubes welded to the chassis frame head.
Early Beetles utilized swing-axle rear suspension, which could result in "jackknifing" or tucking under extreme cornering loads.
Later models adopted independent rear suspension (IRS) utilizing semi-trailing arms, vastly improving handling safety and ride comfort.
The Volkswagen floorpan acts as the structural backbone of the car, allowing body styles like the Karmann Ghia or custom dune buggies to bolt directly onto the chassis.
The Volkswagen Beetle body is bolted to the floorpan with a continuous row of heavy-duty fasteners and sealed with a specialized welting cord.
The classic Volkswagen gearbox casing is cast from magnesium or aluminum, depending on the production era and model type.
Early classic transmissions were non-synchronized on first gear, requiring a double-clutch technique when shifting down into first while moving.
Later transmissions featured full synchronization across all forward gears for smooth, effortless shifting.
Automatic stick-shift transmissions were introduced in the late 1960s, featuring a torque converter paired with a vacuum-operated clutch switch on the gear shift lever.
The classic Volkswagen fuel pump is mechanical, driven by a pushrod riding on a specialized eccentric lobe on the distributor drive gear inside the engine.
The oil temperature in a stock air-cooled Volkswagen relies entirely on the internal oil cooler and airflow over the crankcase, lacking a water thermostat.
In extreme cold weather, air-cooled Volkswagens required specialized pre-heater channels and functional fresh-air systems to defrost the windshield.
The Volkswagen factory in Wolfsburg was heavily fortified during WWII, featuring its own network of underground tunnels and air-raid shelters.
During the British occupation after WWII, workers at the Wolfsburg plant were often paid partly in rations, cigarettes, and hot meals due to currency collapse.
Major Ivan Hirst designed the distinctive blue color used on early post-war military-surplus Volkswagens using leftover paint stocks intended for military radar equipment.
The 1,000,000th Volkswagen built in 1955 was painted in metallic gold and decorated with special gold-plated trim and bumpers.
Volkswagen's global expansion included assembly plants in Nigeria, South Africa, Ireland, New Zealand, and Malaysia.
In Indonesia, Volkswagen assembled variants known as the "Cramayel" and specialized utility vehicles.
The Volkswagen Type 3 was notable for having the lowest profile engine configuration Volkswagen ever produced for air-cooled passenger cars.
The Type 3 "pancake" engine relocated the cooling fan to the end of the crankshaft rather than sitting vertically on top, lowering the engine height dramatically.
The Volkswagen Type 4 introduced unibody construction and McPherson strut front suspension, serving as a technical bridge between old air-cooled designs and modern water-cooled eras.
The Volkswagen Type 4 engine was later adapted for use in Porsche 914 sports cars and Volkswagen-Porsche collaborations.
The Porsche 914, introduced in 1969, used a mid-engine layout powered by either a Volkswagen-derived flat-four or a Porsche flat-six engine.
The Volkswagen Beetle's distinctive sound is generated primarily by the cooling fan and the exhaust pulse from the unequal-length exhaust manifold pipes.
The classic Beetle heater channels run down both structural side sills of the floorpan, making them highly susceptible to rust from moisture trapped inside.
Restoring a classic Volkswagen often involves replacing these structural heater channels and floor pans due to decades of road salt and moisture exposure.
Despite its minimalist engineering, the classic Volkswagen featured innovative touches like a fuel tank designed to deform safely in frontal impacts.
The classic Beetle steering column was engineered with collapsible sections in later years to prevent driver impalement during collisions.
The Volkswagen Beetle became a cultural symbol of thrift, reliability, and counter-culture individuality during the mid-20th century.
Andy Warhol famously featured the Volkswagen Beetle in his 1962 screen print series *Death and Disaster*, highlighting its pervasive presence in American media.
In Woody Allen's 1973 sci-fi comedy film *Sleeper*, a futuristic society discovers a classic Volkswagen Beetle buried in the dirt and successfully starts it up after 200 years.
The last air-cooled Beetle produced in Wolfsburg in 1974 marked the end of volume production in Germany, but output continued abroad for nearly three decades.
The final Mexican-built air-cooled Beetle featured a badge on the rear decklid bearing signatures of factory workers and a commemorative silhouette.
When the final air-cooled Beetle rolled off the Puebla line in 2003, a traditional Mexican mariachi band performed to celebrate the end of production.
The transition from air-cooled to water-cooled engineering saved Volkswagen from financial stagnation, paving the way for global conglomerates like the modern Volkswagen Group.
Today, the Volkswagen Group controls luxury and performance brands including Audi, Porsche, Lamborghini, Bentley, Bugatti, and Ducati.
Despite massive corporate evolution into electric vehicles and multi-brand global empire status, Volkswagen's roots remain tied to Ferdinand Porsche's humble air-cooled design.
Vintage Volkswagen clubs exist in nearly every country on Earth, hosting massive annual gatherings such as "Bug Jam" and "VW Classic."
The air-cooled Volkswagen community remains one of the most dedicated automotive subcultures in history, valuing DIY mechanical simplicity.
The engineering philosophy of the classic Volkswagen prioritized ease of repair, durability, and standardized component interchangeability across decades.
Parts from a 1950 Beetle can often be bolted onto a 1977 Beetle, showcasing unprecedented manufacturing continuity in automotive history.
The simple pushrod architecture of the air-cooled flat-four engine served as the training ground for generations of amateur home mechanics.
The absence of complex electronics in classic air-cooled models means they can be diagnosed and repaired with basic hand tools and a multimeter.
The enduring legacy of the air-cooled Volkswagen is a testament to the brilliant marriage of mass-production scale and robust, timeless engineering.
From its dark origins in pre-war totalitarian planning to its rebirth as a global symbol of peace, mobility, and individuality, Volkswagen's air-cooled era changed the world.
The last air-cooled car produced by Volkswagen—the July 30, 2003 Puebla Beetle—closed the final chapter on over 65 years of continuous air-cooled automotive history.
